readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unobjectionable''' (un-ọb-jek′shọn-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not liable to objection; incapable of being condemned as faulty, false, or improper. ''Paley,'' Evidences, iii. 6.

'''unobjectionably''' (un-ọb-jek′shọn-ạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unobjectionable manner.

'''unobnoxious''' (un-ọb-nok′shus), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not liable; not subject; not exposed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Guardians of Alcinous’ gate
Forever, ''unobnoxious'' to decay.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper,'' Odyssey, vii.}}}}
'''2.''' Not obnoxious; not offensive or hateful.

'''unobsequiousness''' (un-ọb-sē′kwi-us-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being incompliant; want of compliance.
{{smaller block|All ''unobsequiousness'' to the incogitancy.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne,'' Vulg. Err. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unobservable''' (un-ọb-zėr′va-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being observed; not observable; not discoverable. ''Boyle,'' Works, I. 702.

'''unobservance''' (un-ọb-zėr′vans), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or character of being unobservant; want of observation; inattention. ''Whitlock,'' Manners of Eng. People, p. 419.—'''2.''' Lack of compliance with the requirements of some law, rule, or ceremony: as, the ''unobservance'' of the prescribed forms of old law.

'''unobservant''' (un-ọb-zėr′vant), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not observant; not attentive; heedless: as, an ''unobservant'' traveler or reader.
{{smaller block|An unexperienced and ''unobservant'' man.
{{right|''V. Knox,'' Essays, xc.}}}}
'''2.''' Not careful to comply with what is pre-
readings.c1s2:
2. Not careful to comply with what is prescribed or required: as, one ''unobservant'' of etiquette.—'''3.''' Not obsequious. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''unobserved''' (un-ọb-zėrvd′), ''a.'' Not observed; not noticed; not regarded; not heeded.
{{smaller block|''Unobserved'' the glaring orb declines.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, Epil. ii.}}}}

'''unobservedly''' (un-ọb-zėr′ved-li), ''adv.'' In an unobserved manner; without being observed.

'''unobserving''' (un-ọb-zėr′ving), ''a.'' Not observing; inattentive; heedless. ''Waterland'', Works, VI. 176.

'''unobstructed''' (un-ọb-struk′ted), ''a.'' Not obstructed; not filled with impediments; not hindered or stopped; clear: as, an ''unobstructed'' stream or channel. ''Sir R. Blackmore'', Creation, iv.

'''unobstructive''' (un-ọb-struk′tiv), ''a.'' Not presenting any obstacle; not obstructive, in any sense. ''Sir R. Blackmore'', Creation, ii.

'''unobtrusive''' (un-ọb-trö′siv), ''a.'' Not obtrusive; not forward; modest; inconspicuous.
{{smaller block|We possess within our own city an instance of merit, as eminent as it is ''unobtrusive''.
{{right|''E. Everett'', Orations and Speeches, I. 324.}}}}

'''unobtrusively''' (un-ọb-trö′siv-li), ''adv.'' In an unobtrusive manner; not forwardly.

'''unobtrusiveness''' (un-ọb-trö′siv-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unobtrusive.

'''unobvious''' (un-ob′vi-us), ''a.'' Not obvious, evident, or manifest. ''Boyle'', Works, II. 177.

'''unoccupied''' (un-ok′ụ̄-pīd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not occupied; not possessed: as, ''unoccupied'' land. ''N. Grew'',
readings.c1s3:
¶
Cosmologia Sacra.—'''2†.''' Not used; not made use of; unfrequented.

{{smaller block|This way of late had been much ''unoccupied'', and was almost all grown over with grass.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}

'''3.''' Not employed or taken up in business or otherwise: as, ''unoccupied'' time.

'''unode''' (ū′nōd), ''n.'' A conical point of a surface in which the tangent cone has degenerated to two coincident planes, so that infinitely near that point the surface has the form of a thin sheet cut off at an edge, both sides of the sheet being continuous with one side of the surface generally. Also called ''uniplanar node''.

'''unoffending''' (un-ọ-fen′ding), ''a.'' Not offending; not giving offense; not sinning; free from sin or fault; harmless; innocent; blameless.

{{smaller block|<poem>My prayers pull daily blessings on thy head,
My ''unoffending'' child.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, ii.}}}}

'''unoffensive''' (un-ọ-fen′siv), ''a.'' Not offensive; harmless; inoffensive. ''Bp. Fell'', Hammond, i.

'''unofficious''' (un-ọ-fish′us), ''a.'' Not officious; not forward or intermeddling. ''Milton'', Tetrachordon.

'''unoften''' (un-ô′fn), ''adv.'' Not often; rarely. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The man of gallantry not ''unoften'' has been found to think after the same manner. ''Harris'', Three Treatises, ii.}}

{{smaller block|We have good reasons for believing that not ''unoften'' it [the archiepiscopal cross] bore on each of its two sides a figure of our Lord hanging nailed to the rood.
{{right|''Rock'', Church of our Fathers, ii. 233.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
—'''2†.''' Inordinate.
{{smaller block|The delyte that has noghte of ''unordaynde'' styrrynge, and mekely has styrrynge in Criste.
{{right|''MS. Lincoln'' A. i. 17, f. 196. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''unorder''' (un-ôr′dėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''order.''] To counterorder; countermand an order for. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I think I must ''unorder'' the tea.
{{right|''Miss Burney'', Cecilia, viii. 3. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unordered''' (un-ôr′dėrd), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unordred'' (def. 2); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ordered.''] '''1.''' Not in or arranged in order; disordered.—'''2.''' Not ordered or commanded.—'''3.''' Not belonging to a religious order. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thow shalt considere . . . wheither thou be . . . wedded or sengle, ordered or ''unordred.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''unorderly''' (un-ôr′dėr-li), ''a.'' Not orderly; irregular; disorderly. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iv. 4.

'''unordinary''' (un-ôr′di-nạ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not ordinary; not common; unusual.

'''unordinate†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ordinate.''] Inordinate. ''Wyclif'', Ecclus. xlv. 9.

'''unordinately†''', ''adv.'' [ME., < ''unordinate'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Inordinately. ''Wyclif'', 2 Thess. iii. 6.

'''unorganized''' (un-ôr′gan-īzd), ''a.'' Not organized; inorganized; inorganic: as, metals are ''unorganized'' bodies. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 30.
readings.c3s2:
''Coventry'', Philemon to Hyde, v.

¶
'''unorthodox''' (un-ôr′thọ̄-doks), ''a.'' Not orthodox; heterodox; heretical. ''Decay of Christian Piety.''

'''unorthodoxy''' (un-ôr′thọ̄-dok-si), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unorthodox; unsoundness in faith; heterodoxy; heresy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Calvin made roast-meat of Servetus at Geneva for his ''unorthodoxy''. ''Tom Brown'', Works, III. 104. (''Davies.'')}}

'''unossified''' (un-os′i-fīd), ''a.'' Not ossified; not bony: specifically noting structures which usually become bone in the course of time, or in other cases.

'''unostentatious''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not ostentatious; not boastful; not making show or parade; modest. ''West'', On the Resurrection. —'''2.''' Not glaring; not showy: as, ''unostentatious'' coloring.

'''unostentatiously''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus-li), ''adv.'' In an unostentatious manner; without show, parade, or ostentation. ''V. Knox.''

'''unostentatiousness''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unostentatious, or free from ostentation.

'''unowed''' (un-ōd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not owed; not due. —'''2†.''' Not owned; having no owner.
{{smaller block|<poem>England now is left
To tug and scamble, and to part by the teeth
The ''unowed'' interest of proud-swelling state.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3. 147.}}}}

'''unowned<sup>1</sup>''' (un-ōnd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''owned'', pp. of ''own''<sup>1</sup>.] Not owned; having no known owner; not claimed. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 407.

'''Unogata†''' (ū-nọ̄-gā′tä), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Fabricius, 1775).] In the Fabrician classification, a division of insects having only maxillary palpi, including the dragon-flies, centipeds, and spiders.

'''unoil''' (un-oil′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''oil.''] To free from oil. ''Dryden.''

'''unoiled''' (un-oild′), ''a.'' Not oiled; free from oil.
{{smaller block|''Unoiled'' hinges.{{right|''Young'', Love of Fame, vi.}}}}

'''unold†''' (un-ōld′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''old.''] To make young; rejuvenate.
{{smaller block|Minde-gladding fruit that can ''unolde'' a man.{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Schisme.}}}}

'''Unona''' (ū-nō′nä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus filius, 1781); altered from NL. ''Anona'', the name of a related genus.] A genus of plants, of the order ''Anonaceæ'', type of the tribe ''Unoneæ.'' {{smaller|It differs from ''Asimina'', the papaw of the United States, in its commonly moniliform fruit, and from others of its tribe in its corolla with flat open petals, and in having numerous ovules in a single series. The 25 species are natives of tropical Asia, except 4 or 5 which are African. They are trees or shrubby climbers, usually with large flowers solitary in or near the axils, their petals often 2 or 3 inches long, reaching 6 inches in ''U. longiflora'', a shrub of Assam. Their young branches are often silky or velvety, with brown, gray, golden, or reddish hairs, or, in ''U. Desmos'' and ''U. discolor'', are covered with white dots or tubercles. Many species yield an aromatic bark and fruit, used as a stimulant and febrifuge. ''U. discolor'', cultivated in India, and native also in China and the Malay archipelago, is a small tree or shrub with polymorphous leaves, odorous yellow flowers with silky petals in several varieties, and purple moniliform fruit with fleshy joints, resembling small grapes; from the unripe fruit the Chinese make a purple dye. ''U. viridiflora'', a gigantic climber of Indian forests, is remarkable for the bright-green color of its large flowers. For the former ''U. hamata'', now ''Artabotrys odoratissima'', see ''tail-grape''; for the former ''U.'' (now ''Cananga'') ''odorata'', see ''Cananga''. See also ''Uvaria'' and ''Xylopia'', with which the species have been much confused.}}

'''Unoneæ''' (ū-nō′nē-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Bentham and Hooker, 1862), < ''Unona'' + ''-eæ''.] A tribe of polypetalous plants, of the order ''Anonaceæ'', characterized by flowers with densely crowded stamens and six valvate flattened or connivent petals in two rows, all nearly alike, or the inner small or absent. {{smaller|It includes 16 genera, of which ''Unona'' is the type; ''Asimina'' and ''Trigyneia'' are American, the others natives mostly of tropical Asia or Africa.}}

'''unoperative''' (un-op′e̤-rā̤-tiv), ''a.'' Inoperative.
{{smaller block|If the life of Christ be hid to this world, much more is his Scepter ''unoperative'' but in spirituall things.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}

'''unoperculate, unoperculated''' (un-ọ̄-pėr′kụ̄-lāt, -lā-ted), ''a.'' Inoperculate.

'''unopposed''' (un-ọ-pōzd′), ''a.'' Not opposed; not resisted; not meeting with obstruction.
{{smaller block|For what end was that bill to linger beyond the usual period of an ''unopposed'' measure?
{{right|''Burke'', Speech at Bristol, 1789.}}}}
'''Unopposed blow.''' {{smaller|See ''blow''<sup>3</sup>.}}

'''unoppressive''' (un-ọ-pres′iv), ''a.'' Not oppressive. ''Burke'', French Rev.

'''uno-rail''' (ū′nō-rāl), ''a.'' [Irreg. < L. ''unus'', one, + E. ''rail''<sup>1</sup>.] Characterized by a single rail: noting a traction system for ordinary wagons, in which a single rail is laid for the locomotive, which grasps it by means of paired driving-wheels set almost horizontally. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''unordained''' (un-ôr-dānd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not ordained. —'''2†.''' Inordinate.
{{smaller block|The delyte that has noghte of ''unordaynde'' styrrynge, and mekely has styrrynge in Criste.
{{right|''MS. Lincoln'' A. i. 17, f. 196. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''unorder''' (un-ôr′dėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''order.''] To counterorder; countermand an order for. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I think I must ''unorder'' the tea.
{{right|''Miss Burney'', Cecilia, viii. 3. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unordered''' (un-ôr′dėrd), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unordred'' (def. 2); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ordered.''] '''1.''' Not in or arranged in order; disordered.—'''2.''' Not ordered or commanded.—'''3.''' Not belonging to a religious order. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thow shalt considere . . . wheither thou be . . . wedded or sengle, ordered or ''unordred.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''unordinary''' (un-ôr′di-nạ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not ordinary; not common; unusual.

'''unordinate†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ordinate.''] Inordinate. ''Wyclif'', Ecclus. xlv. 9.

'''unordinately†''', ''adv.'' [ME., < ''unordinate'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Inordinately. ''Wyclif'', 2 Thess. iii. 6.

'''unorganized''' (un-ôr′gan-īzd), ''a.'' Not organized; inorganized; inorganic: as, metals are ''unorganized'' bodies. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 30.

'''unoriginal''' (un-ọ̄-rij′i-na̤l), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not original; derived; adventitious; accidental.—'''2.''' Having no origin or birth; ungenerated.
{{smaller block|''Unoriginal'' night and chaos wild. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 477.}}

'''unoriginate''' (un-ọ̄-rij′i-nāt), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''originate'', a., < ML. ''originatus'', pp.: see ''originate'', ''v.''] Not originated.
{{smaller block|Arius denied of Christ that He was ''unoriginate'', or part of the ''Unoriginate''. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 537.}}}}

'''unoriginated''' (un-ọ̄-rij′i-nā-ted), ''a.'' Not originated; having no birth or creation.
{{smaller block|The Father alone is self-existent, underived, ''unoriginated''. {{right|''Waterland'', Works, II. 348.}}}}

'''unoriginatedness''' (un-ọ̄-rij′i-nā-ted-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unoriginated or without birth or creation.
{{smaller block|Self-existence or ''unoriginatedness''.
{{right|''Waterland'', Works, III. 120.}}}}

'''unoriginately''' (un-ọ̄-rij′i-nāt-li), ''adv.'' Without birth or origin.
{{smaller block|He is so emphatically or ''unoriginately''.
{{right|''Waterland'', Works, II. 29.}}}}

'''unorn†''', '''unorne†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''unourne'', < AS. *''unorne'' (in ''unornlīc''), old.] Old; worn out; feeble.
{{smaller block|<poem>I waxe feble and ''vnourne'';
To flee to God is my beste way.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 70.}}}}

'''unornamental''' (un-ôr-na̤-men′ta̤l), ''a.'' Not ornamental. ''West'', On the Resurrection, p. 335.

'''unornamented''' (un-ôr′na̤-men-ted), ''a.'' Not ornamented; unadorned; not decorated; plain. ''Coventry'', Philemon to Hyde, v.

'''unorthodox''' (un-ôr′thọ̄-doks), ''a.'' Not orthodox; heterodox; heretical. ''Decay of Christian Piety.''

'''unorthodoxy''' (un-ôr′thọ̄-dok-si), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unorthodox; unsoundness in faith; heterodoxy; heresy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Calvin made roast-meat of Servetus at Geneva for his ''unorthodoxy''. ''Tom Brown'', Works, III. 104. (''Davies.'')}}

'''unossified''' (un-os′i-fīd), ''a.'' Not ossified; not bony: specifically noting structures which usually become bone in the course of time, or in other cases.

'''unostentatious''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not ostentatious; not boastful; not making show or parade; modest. ''West'', On the Resurrection. —'''2.''' Not glaring; not showy: as, ''unostentatious'' coloring.

'''unostentatiously''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus-li), ''adv.'' In an unostentatious manner; without show, parade, or ostentation. ''V. Knox.''

'''unostentatiousness''' (un-os-ten-tā′shus-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unostentatious, or free from ostentation.

'''unowed''' (un-ōd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not owed; not due. —'''2†.''' Not owned; having no owner.
{{smaller block|<poem>England now is left
To tug and scamble, and to part by the teeth
The ''unowed'' interest of proud-swelling state.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3. 147.}}}}

'''unowned<sup>1</sup>''' (un-ōnd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''owned'', pp. of ''own''<sup>1</sup>.] Not owned; having no known owner; not claimed. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 407.

'''unowned<sup>2</sup>''' (un-ōnd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''owned'', pp. of ''own''<sup>2</sup>.] Not avowed; not acknowledged as one’s own; not admitted as done by one’s self; unconfessed: as, ''unowned'' faults. ''Gay'', Trivia, ii.

'''unpack''' (un-pak′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pack''.] '''1.''' To open, as things packed: as, to ''unpack'' goods.—'''2.''' To relieve of a pack or burden; unload; disburden.

'''unpacker''' (un-pak′ėr), ''n.'' One who unpacks. ''Miss Edgeworth'', Ennui, iii. (''Davies.'')

'''unpaid''' (un-pād′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not paid; not discharged, as a debt. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 782.—'''2.''' Not having received what is due: as, ''unpaid'' workmen.
{{smaller block|If her armies are three years ''unpaid'', she is the less exhausted by expense.
{{right|''Burke'', State of the Nation.}}}}
'''3.''' Serving without pay; unsalaried: as, ''unpaid'' justices.—'''Unpaid-for''', {{smaller|not paid for.}}
{{smaller block|Prouder than rustling in ''unpaid-for'' silk.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 3. 24.}}}}

'''unpained''' (un-pānd′), ''a.'' Not pained; suffering no pain. ''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.

'''unpainful''' (un-pān′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not painful; giving no pain.
{{smaller block|An easy and ''unpainful'' touch.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 4.}}}}

'''unpaint''' (un-pānt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''paint''.] To efface the painting or color of. ''Parnell.''

'''unpaired''' (un-pãrd′), ''a.'' Not paired, in any sense.—'''Unpaired fins''', {{smaller|of fishes the vertical fins—namely, the dorsal, anal, and caudal.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
